item.title: Accord: Schelling-Point Arbitration as a Composable Solana Primitive
item.description: arXiv:2610.20666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accord is an arbitration oracle on Solana. Any Solana program can create an application specific court (i.e. subaccord) and file disputes. A random jury of a specialized, stake-weighted juror pool reviews encrypted evidence and votes under commit--reveal. Jurors that vote with the final ruling earn fees and slashed stake. Jurors that vote against it lose stake. Appeals grow the panel stepwise from 3 to 31 jurors, which raises both the cost of maintaining a captured verdict and, under certain conditions, the probability of a correct majority. Each pool defines its own collateral mint and its own fee mint, so the economics can fit the application. This paper elaborates the mechanism, the incentive model, the residual trust assumptions, and the differences to the established court on EVM, Kleros. We further discuss implementation details that are Solana specific.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Schuh

item.title: Approximating the Value of Time-Bounded Weighted Timed Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.21487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Value Problem for weighted timed games, an extension of timed automata with weights and adversity, consists in determining, given a weighted timed game with a reachability objective and a rational threshold, whether or not the value of the game exceeds the threshold. This problem is known to be undecidable for weighted timed games, i.e., there is no algorithm that can compute the value exactly. A natural alternative is to approximate the value; however, the Approximation problem is also undecidable in general. In this paper, we prove that the Approximation problem is decidable in 4-ExpTime for weighted timed games whose executions are time-bounded.
item.dc:creator: Isa Vialard, Jo\"el Ouaknine

item.title: How language model agents reshape price competition
item.description: arXiv:2610.21711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Repeated Bertrand competition is a stringent benchmark for algorithmic pricing: in homogeneous-goods markets, standard learning procedures typically select the stage-game Nash outcome with prices near marginal cost. We show that LLM pricing agents can escape this benchmark, depending on deployment decisions. LLMs outperform standard online learners through faster adaptation, but this advantage largely disappears against full-information learners. An extracted surrogate algorithm illustrates how LLMs in specific deployments profit from regularly undercutting slower learners. Agents that post one price every period from raw market histories that include rival prices can sustain supracompetitive regimes in self-play. Agents that periodically emit probability distributions from summarized histories of their own profits instead move toward the competitive region in self-play. Markets mixing these interfaces can generate dynamic regimes in which LLMs establish a high-price anchor and regularly undercut it to capture demand. These regimes can keep both competitors' prices above marginal cost. Deployment choices shape these outcomes, shifting the focus from stationary equilibria to dynamic pricing regimes.
item.dc:creator: Martin Bichler, Philip Hierhager, Kassian K\"ock, Fabian Pieroth

item.title: Learning Rewards in Strategic Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.21912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Bergerault, Cyrille Kone, Giorgia Ramponi

item.title: Why Alternation Speeds Up Counterfactual Regret Minimization?
item.description: arXiv:2610.21970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solving imperfect-information games at scale rests on counterfactual regret minimization with the regret matching$^{+}$ (RM$^{+}$) update, and a seemingly minor implementation choice accounts for much of its practical speed: alternating the two players' updates, so that the second player responds to the strategy the first player just produced. A widely repeated intuition explains why: seeing the opponent's fresh strategy should act like optimism. We treat this intuition as a testable hypothesis about deterministic two-player zero-sum self-play dynamics and find that its canonical additive form fails an information-matched test. On an analytic witness family we compare alternating RM$^{+}$ against a one-sided predictive RM$^{+}$ that receives the same information channel each round and differs only in where the fresh signal enters, a persistent regret state versus a transient prediction term. Our main result is a dichotomy theorem that reduces trajectory separation to the recurrence of exact-vertex play by the predictive dynamics: under an interior-band assumption on the alternating iterate, either vertex times recur and the profile distance is at least, infinitely often, an explicit constant that our measurements nearly attain, or they terminate. Across the tested self-play regimes, any correct explanation of the alternation speedup must reproduce a staleness cost present at the smallest tested stale fraction, an advantage that persists across seven orders of payoff conditioning, regime crossings of the optimism family, and a measured per-perturbation cost of weakening the injection path that is far steeper for staleness than for partial persistence.
item.dc:creator: Boning Li, Longbo Huang

item.title: Smoothed analysis of policy iteration and value iteration for deterministic discounted and mean-payoff games played on any graph
item.description: arXiv:2610.22149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Our understanding of turn-based stochastic games is reminiscent of our understanding of linear programming in the 1970s. Instead of the simplex method, we have two families of algorithms - policy iteration and value iteration - which work well in practice but are known to run in exponential time on some input instances, and we still lack an algorithm that runs in polynomial time on all instances. A recent result by Loff and Skomra showed that, for deterministic discounted and mean-payoff games played on an ergodic graph, a variant of policy iteration runs in smoothed polynomial time. This offered an explanation of why policy iteration performs well in practice, analogous to Spielman and Teng's explanation for the simplex method. In this paper, we drop the ergodicity assumption: we show that their policy iteration algorithms run in smoothed polynomial time for any game graph. We do this by defining a condition number that naturally generalizes theirs, showing that sufficiently-perturbed games are well-conditioned with high probability, and showing that their algorithms are efficient on well-conditioned instances. Although the outline is similar, our proof requires a substantially new approach, based on log-Lipschitz distributions which recently appeared in work on the smoothed analysis of the simplex method. For our second contribution, we propose three new value iteration algorithms for solving deterministic mean-payoff games (also on any graph). All three are based on iterative methods for finding fixed points of non-expansive operators, which we show can be applied to the Shapley operator. The first two are simple applications of Krasnoselskii-Mann iteration and Halpern iteration. The third is quadratically faster but more complicated: it runs Zwick-Paterson and Halpern iterations in parallel. We prove that all three algorithms are correct and run in smoothed polynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Bruno Loff, Mateusz Skomra

item.title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
item.description: arXiv:2610.22201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs.
item.dc:creator: Ian Gemp, Shubhendu Trivedi, Adam Fisch, Fantine Huot, Michael Kaisers, Mirella Lapata, William W. Cohen, Alekh Agarwal, Kate Larson, Jacob Eisenstein

item.title: Market Incentives for AI Safety Investment
item.description: arXiv:2610.21607v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Despite their practical significance, modern AI systems pose significant societal risks, including toxicity, malicious use, and misinformation. Their mitigation depends not only on technical feasibility but also on the incentives of firms that develop and deploy these systems. We show how profit maximization shapes safety investment in an AI supply chain with an upstream LLM provider and several competing downstream firms. In our game-theoretic model, we derive the market-driven level of safety investment and compare it with the levels that maximize market welfare and industry profit. We find that downstream competition generally induces downstream firms to invest more in safety than the industry-profit-optimal level. By contrast, the upstream provider may underinvest relative to these benchmarks because it is not fully compensated for the surplus from safety investments. Finally, we analyze how different regulatory interventions affect the participants' incentives and profits, and the resulting levels of model safety.
item.dc:creator: Nikita Tsoy

item.title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines
item.description: arXiv:2610.22277v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.
item.dc:creator: Florian Lercher, Karan Mahesh, Yujun Huang, Meshal Alharbi, Runyu Zhang, Hanna Krasowski, Michael R. Benjamin, Matthias Althoff, Gioele Zardini

item.title: Switchback Price Experiments with Forward-Looking Demand
item.description: arXiv:2410.14904v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Switchback experiments are widely used in pricing applications. We consider a retailer running such an experiment for the price of a single product, with infinite supply. In each period, the seller chooses a price from a set of predefined prices consisting of an original price and a few discounted price levels. The goal is to estimate the demand gradient at the original price to adjust the original price and improve revenue after the experiment. In our model, in each period, a unit mass of buyers arrives on the market, with values distributed based on a time-varying process. Crucially, buyers are forward-looking with a discounted utility and will choose not to purchase now if they expect to face a discounted price in the near future. We show that such forward-looking behavior introduces bias in naive estimators of the demand gradient, due to intertemporal interference. Furthermore, although experiments with only two price points are common in practice, we prove that no estimator using data from such experiments can recover the correct demand gradient, even in the limit of an infinitely long experiment with an infinitesimal price discount. Moreover, we characterize the form of the bias of naive estimators. Finally, we show that with a simple three-price-level experiment, the seller can remove the bias due to strategic forward-looking behavior and construct an estimator for the demand gradient that asymptotically recovers the truth. Our results provide practical guidance for platforms to obtain unbiased demand gradients from price experiments in the presence of forward-looking demand.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Wu, Ramesh Johari, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Gabriel Y. Weintraub

item.title: Infinite lexicographic products of positional objectives
item.description: arXiv:2506.14544v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper contributes to the study of positional determinacy of infinite duration games played on potentially infinite graphs with neutral transitions. Recently, [Ohlmann, TheoretiCS 2023] established that positionality of prefix-independent objectives is preserved by finite lexicographic products. We propose two different notions of infinite lexicographic products indexed by arbitrary ordinals, and extend Ohlmann's result by proving that they also preserve positionality. In the context of one-player positionality, this extends positional determinacy results of [Gr\"adel and Walukiewicz, Logical Methods in Computer Science 2006] to edge-labelled games and arbitrarily many priorities for both Max-Parity and Min-Parity. Moreover, we show that the Max-Parity objectives over countable ordinals are complete for the infinite levels of the difference hierarchy over $\Sigma^0_2$ and that Min-Parity is complete for the class $\Sigma^0_3$. We obtain therefore positional languages that are complete for all those levels, as well as new insights about closure under unions and neutral letters.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Casares, Pierre Ohlmann, Micha{\l} Skrzypczak, Igor Walukiewicz

item.title: Introspectively Envy-Free and Efficient Allocation of Indivisible Mixed Manna
item.description: arXiv:2509.18673v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The existence of allocations that are simultaneously fair and efficient is a central inquiry in fair division. Prominent results show that these complementary desiderata can be achieved together for indivisible items with nonnegative values. In particular, for indivisible goods and additive valuations, there always exists an allocation that is both envy-free up to one item (EF1) and fractionally Pareto efficient (fPO). An analogous EF1 and fPO guarantee is now known for indivisible chores. For indivisible mixed manna, the compatibility of fairness and efficiency is more delicate. Indeed, recent work shows that EF1 and fPO are incompatible in the additive mixed-manna setting. Through principled relaxations of EF1, we show that compatibility with fPO can be restored even for indivisible mixed manna under additive valuations. For indivisible mixed manna and additive valuations, we establish the existence of allocations that are fPO and introspectively envy-free up to one item (IEF1). In an IEF1 allocation, each agent can eliminate its envy toward every other agent by either adding an item to or removing an item from its own bundle. The notion of IEF1 coincides with EF1 for indivisible chores, and hence our result generalizes the existence guarantee for chores. We also prove the existence of allocations that are fPO and satisfy a chiral version of IEF1, which we call extrospectively envy-free up to one item (XEF1). This result generalizes the existence guarantee of EF1 and fPO allocations for goods, since XEF1 is equivalent to EF1 for goods. Finally, we utilize our IEF1 and fPO result for indivisible items to provide a distinct proof of the known EF and fPO guarantee for divisible mixed manna. Our results underscore the power of the Knaster--Kuratowski--Mazurkiewicz Theorem for proving the existence of fair and efficient allocations of indivisible and divisible items.
item.dc:creator: Siddharth Barman, Paritosh Verma

item.title: How Hard Is It to Rig a Tournament When Few Players Can Beat or Be Beaten by the Favorite?
item.description: arXiv:2601.08530v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In knockout tournaments, players compete in successive rounds, with losers eliminated and winners advancing until a single champion remains. Given a tournament digraph $D$, which encodes the outcomes of all possible matches, and a designated player $v^* \in V(D)$, the \textsc{Tournament Fixing} problem (TFP) asks whether the tournament can be scheduled in a way that guarantees $v^*$ emerges as the winner. TFP is known to be NP-hard, but is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by structural measures such as the feedback arc set (fas) or feedback vertex set (fvs) number of the tournament digraph. In this paper, we introduce and study two new structural parameters: the number of players who can defeat $v^*$ (i.e., the in-degree of $v^*$, denoted by $k$) and the number of players that $v^*$ can defeat (i.e., the out-degree of $v^*$, denoted by $\ell$). A natural question is that: can TFP be efficiently solved when $k$ or $\ell$ is small? We answer this question affirmatively by showing that TFP is FPT when parameterized by either the in-degree or out-degree of $v^*$. Our algorithm for the in-degree parameterization is particularly involved and technically intricate. Notably, the in-degree $k$ can remain small even when other structural parameters, such as fas or fvs, are large. Hence, our results offer a new perspective and significantly broaden the parameterized algorithmic understanding of the \textsc{Tournament Fixing} problem.
item.dc:creator: Zhonghao Wang, Junqiang Peng, Yuxi Liu, Mingyu Xiao

item.title: Characterization and Computation of Normal-Form Proper Equilibria in Extensive-Form Games via the Sequence-Form Representation
item.description: arXiv:2602.10524v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Normal-form proper equilibrium, introduced by Myerson as a refinement of normal-form perfect equilibrium, plays an important role in the equilibrium analysis of extensive-form games because of its stronger stability properties. However, the exponential growth of the normal-form representation makes existing approaches for directly computing normal-form proper equilibria computationally impractical. To address this challenge, we introduce sequence-form proper equilibrium by defining a maximal payoff function over sequences, and prove its strategic equivalence to normal-form proper equilibrium. For computation, we further derive an equivalent formulation of sequence-form proper equilibrium via a class of perturbed games in sequence form, in which the perturbed realization-plan space is induced by imposing probability lower bounds on restricted sequence sets to encode the desired perturbation hierarchy. Based on this formulation, we develop two differentiable path-following methods for computing normal-form proper equilibria. These methods rely on artificial sequence-form games in which the expected payoff functions are regularized by logarithmic or entropy terms through an auxiliary variable. For each method, as the auxiliary variable tends to zero, the limit point of the induced smooth equilibrium path can derive one or more normal-form proper equilibria of the original game. Finally, Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Yuqing Hou, Yiyin Cao, Chuangyin Dang

item.title: Equitable Auctions
item.description: arXiv:2403.07799v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study how auction design shapes surplus division among bidders. We introduce a parsimonious ex post equity notion and examine standard multi-unit auctions. The equity-optimal pricing depends sharply on the private-common value composition. Among mixed-price auctions, at one extreme, uniform pricing is always optimal for pure common values and, at the other, pay-as-bid pricing is preferred for pure private values under standard regularity assumptions. For any fixed monotone allocation rule, we characterize a BNIC interim-IR implementation that equalizes surplus ex post across all bidders and is revenue-maximizing among those that equalize surplus ex ante; efficient allocation permits parity among winners.
item.dc:creator: Simon Finster, Patrick Loiseau, Simon Mauras, Mathieu Molina, Bary Pradelski

item.title: Tourist arrival forecasting with game-theoretic social influence weighting and deep learning
item.description: arXiv:2507.03411v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the era of Industry 5.0, data-driven decision-making has become indispensable for planning in service systems such as tourism. This paper proposes a non-linear hybrid approach for forecasting tourist arrivals to Hong Kong from five major source markets before COVID-19 and to Sanya, China, through the COVID-19 shock. The method integrates multiple sources of Internet big data and employs a cooperative game-theoretic algorithm to identify coalitions of opinion leaders on social media, whose content then receives larger weights. The Empirical Wavelet Transform (EWT), applied causally, manages nonstationary attributes, and a Stacked Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (Stacked BiLSTM) network tuned by Bayesian optimization generates the forecasts. We prove that the Shapley values of the underlying trust-weighted coverage game have a closed form and that the coalition of maximal synergy can be found exactly in polynomial time. Relative to the same network fed only with past arrivals, Internet big data reduce the one-step-ahead root mean squared error by 4.1-41.7% across the Hong Kong markets and opinion-leader weighting by a further 10.1-49.4%, against 5.3% and 8.7% for Sanya. The approach compares favorably with published benchmarks and remains robust under volatile conditions, which suggests uses in logistics, supply chains and production planning.
item.dc:creator: Ali Nikseresht
